transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-11-23 16:00 UTC, Duration: 48m, Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Raj Patel (Redwood SE); Emily Torres (Auriga CTO); Liam O'Neill (Auriga ML Eng); Priya Sharma (Auriga Infra)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll keep to 45 minutes, quick agenda recap, results v baseline, routing playbook, next steps, questions
[00:23] Emily Torres: thanks, Maya. quick note — got Priya and Liam here to focus on infra & bench. we saw the first-day numbers, want to understand tail behavior more than averages
[00:40] Raj Patel: yep makes sense. i pulled the runs side-by-side: our median token latency was 42ms on Seq-128 workload, incumbent reported 65ms median under their infra; but the 99p was where things diverged — we hit 210ms, incumbent hit about 540ms in their report
[01:05] Liam O'Neill: okay, that 99p delta sounds promising but is that with KV cache warm? our production traffic has a lot of cold prefixes so need to see cold-start tails
[01:22] Raj Patel: good call — the runs I showed are with prefix caching enabled and a warm KV snapshot. we also have a cold-run in the sheet where our 99p is 720ms vs incumbent 1.1s, so still better but closer
[01:45] Priya Sharma: could you repeat the hardware profiles? i want to make sure we're comparing apples; the incumbent said they use mixed vGPU pools
[02:01] Raj Patel: sure — these runs used r-infer-a100-80g equivalents, batch size tuned to 8 for latency SLO, and continuous batching window of 12ms. incumbent's public notes imply larger batching and higher concurrency which pushes their median up on short sequences, weirdly
[02:28] Emily Torres: hmm our main concern is throughput for peak overnight ingest — bursts that saturate concurrency. how did Redwood behave when concurrency hit 250 concurrent requests?
[02:42] Raj Patel: we ran a staged ramp; at 250 concurrent, our throughput paused briefly due to autoscale cold starts if the KV snapshot needed to repopulate. with the routing policy we propose, those heavy tails are mitigated by splitting long-contexts to dedicated slots — overall 8-12% throughput uplift and 25% improvement in 99p
[03:12] Liam O'Neill: split long-contexts to dedicated slots — can you explain that config? i'm not sure I follow the slot assignment logic
[03:25] Raj Patel: yeah — essentially workload classification at the routing layer: small context (<512 tokens) -> high-throughput pool with aggressive batching; long context (>=512 tokens) -> dedicated slots that have higher kv cache affinity and pre-warm windows. fallback rule if dedicated is saturated: route to compressed quantized variant with slightly higher latency but much lower memory
[03:55] Priya Sharma: that fallback to quantized variant — what's the accuracy delta? any hallucination or generation drift observed?
[04:04] Raj Patel: we ran evals on our tuning set, ROUGE/EM like metrics showed <1.5% degradation on average for the 4-bit profile we used, worst-case ~3% on very long summarization prompts. i can share the eval sheet. it's a tradeoff but for background processing it's acceptable
[04:34] Emily Torres: right, some of our UIs surface suggestions to clinicians — we can't tolerate visible regressions. so maybe fallback only for async batch jobs, not UI flows
[04:45] Maya Chen: noted — routing can be route-tag aware. we can set X-user-visible boolean so UI-level requests never go to quantized fallback. raj will include that in the playbook
[04:58] Raj Patel: yeah we'll show the policy snippet. also importantly, the incumbent uses wide batching for most routes which increases median under small sequences; we tune to smaller micro-batches to keep medians low
[05:19] Liam O'Neill: what about token-cost? incumbent quoted lower per-token last month, is your cost per token comparable once we add dedicated slot charges?
[05:31] Maya Chen: short answer: depends on mix. hosted on-demand could be slightly cheaper on pure tokens, but when you factor in lower token waste due to cache hit improvements and fewer retries from lower tail latencies, the unit cost can be lower with Redwood. dedicated slots add fixed monthly but give predictable throughput and lower p99 penalties
[05:57] Priya Sharma: in the sheets we saw a weird spike at 18:22 during the 6h run — memory thrash?
[06:06] Raj Patel: yes that was a misconfigured cache eviction policy in our early run — fixed in later runs. the corrected runs exclude that spike. the logs are annotated in the shared folder
[06:20] Emily Torres: thanks. okay, can we dig into the 24h run you want us to perform — what specifically should we validate beyond p50/p99?
[06:32] Raj Patel: great question — please surface per-route token distribution, cold vs warm prefix rates, error rates by model variant, and tail latency percentiles (p90/p95/p99/p999 if possible). also capture model fallback counts. we provided a run-template in the drive
[06:51] Liam O'Neill: note — our traffic pattern includes scheduled batch jobs that submit long contexts during midnight window; we'll simulate that in the 24h test
[06:58] Maya Chen: perfect. quick comment on routing - we've added a reactive fallback: if average 99p across the pool > 800ms for 3 consecutive minutes, route new requests to the quantized variant for up to 5 minutes while autoscale stabilizes
[07:18] Priya Sharma: sounds good. one security question — when you said KV cache snapshot, where is that snapshot stored? we need encryption at rest and KMS integration
[07:27] Raj Patel: snapshot resides in the customer's controlled S3 bucket in the private deployment option; for Hosted we use encrypted object storage with KMS customer-managed keys available for Redwood Private. i can link SOC 2 & KMS docs after the call
[07:45] Emily Torres: please do, Priya will audit that.
[07:49] Maya Chen: moving on, we noticed the incumbent's throughput dropped dramatically when model drift required reloading new weights; do you have graceful rollback?
[07:58] Raj Patel: yes, we support canary rollouts and instant fallback to previous model snapshot with zero downtime pattern — it keeps serving capacity while weights stream. in our bench we toggled versions and saw <200ms additional latency during the swap window
[08:18] Liam O'Neill: how reproducible are your numbers across regions? we're running EU and US; incumbent's EU latency is worse for us
[08:28] Raj Patel: numbers are region-local; the playbook includes region-based routing and multi-region fallback. EU runs show median ~55ms vs incumbent 85ms in our tests — but depends on available GPU types and network egress
[08:45] Emily Torres: okay. one more — quantization: you mentioned 4-bit. any plans for 3-bit or specialized kernels that affect latency?
[08:54] Raj Patel: we have an experimental 3-bit candidate but it's early and shows more variability on long sequences. it helps throughput but can increase p99 unpredictably; not recommended for user-facing flows yet
[09:12] Maya Chen: shifting to results slide 5 — the mixed workload sim where we had 60% short, 30% medium, 10% long — Redwood median 48ms, incumbent 72ms, throughput at steady-state we saw +12% qps on our setup
[09:34] Priya Sharma: i see you flagged a higher error rate on the longest-context variant, what's root cause?
[09:41] Raj Patel: that was due to tokenization edge cases combined with retries — fixed by aligning tokenizer config and adding a strong preflight validation. we pushed patched runs after that fix
[09:55] Liam O'Neill: on autoscale — what's warm pool sizing recommendation for our expected peak of 400 RPS?
[10:05] Raj Patel: recommend baseline dedicated slots for 200 RPS with burst autoscale to add 150-250% for spikes; the playbook contains exact formulas based on observed tokens-per-request distribution
[10:21] Emily Torres: will that autoscale add cold-start penalty frequently? our SLO is p99 < 600ms for UI latency flows
[10:29] Raj Patel: with pre-warm windows and predictive scaling based on time-series, cold-start events can be limited to rare maintenance windows. for UI flows we suggest pinning to dedicated high-affinity slots to avoid cold starts entirely
[10:48] Maya Chen: quick interruption — Liam, you had a question about datasets and eval coverage?
[10:53] Liam O'Neill: yeah, do your eval sets include our clinical summarization prompts? i want to ensure evals are representative
[11:01] Raj Patel: we included a subset of your provided prompts; for confidentiality some were obfuscated but distribution preserved. we agree we need a larger slice from you — can we get another 200 samples for eval?
[11:14] Emily Torres: yes, security-approved subset, we'll send by EOD Friday.
[11:20] Priya Sharma: regarding logs — what telemetry do you need from our side? structured traces, token-level timing, or just per-request latency?
[11:30] Raj Patel: token-level timing is ideal but per-request latency with start/end and model-variant tag is acceptable. also include route tag and any user-visible flag so we can correlate fallbacks
[11:42] Maya Chen: switching to the incident from yesterday — Emily reported a 502 cascade when a large batch flooded the ingress
[11:50] Emily Torres: yeah it caused 5 minutes of elevated errors. the incumbent's retry logic compounded it, so our client retried and made it worse
[11:59] Raj Patel: our retry policy differs; we put exponential backoff and circuit breaker at gateway. in the bench we simulated retries and Redwood had graceful degradation with 20% fewer client retries observed
[12:17] Liam O'Neill: can you share the circuit breaker config? we may want to implement similar logic on client side
[12:23] Raj Patel: will include config snippet in playbook (thresholds, cooldown, backoff windows)
[12:30] Maya Chen: quick poll — anyone strongly opposed to running the 24h test in staging with the playbook applied?
[12:37] Emily Torres: no objections from me
[12:40] Priya Sharma: go ahead, but we'll sandbox and monitor closely
[12:44] Liam O'Neill: agreed
[12:46] Maya Chen: ok great. action items recap: raj produce playbook and config diffs, maya pricing note, liam run 24h, emily send eval prompts. anything else?
[12:58] Emily Torres: one ask — can Redwood provide a short runbook for SREs on how to interpret fallback counts and when to escalate?
[13:06] Raj Patel: yes we'll add SRE runbook appendix with escalation thresholds and logs to capture
[13:12] Maya Chen: i'll set up exec check-in the week of 12/07 once we have 24h results and cost delta
[13:18] Priya Sharma: can you also include a brief security checklist for private deployment vs hosted?
[13:24] Raj Patel: yep — KMS options, audit log retention, VPC peering notes, and HSM options for private installs
[13:33] Liam O'Neill: switching back — there's a small flub in the transcript, did you say 3% worst-case accuracy loss at 4-bit?
[13:41] Raj Patel: yes worst-case ~3% on long summarizations, typically under 1.5% on shorter prompts
[13:48] Emily Torres: thanks. anything else on perf?
[13:51] Maya Chen: only final note — we recommend starting the staging 24h window Monday night to hit your long-batch midnight window in the test. agree?
[14:00] Liam O'Neill: that's perfect
[14:03] Maya Chen: okay wrapping up. thanks all, we'll circulate artifacts and timeline.
